clue.text: He's in order, refusing to speak

definitions.text: He's in order, refusing to speak

parts.words: He's in order, refusing to speak
parts.note: 'in order' reads as tidy, but means belonging to a religious order whose monks keep a rule of silence

explanation.surface: Someone who is perfectly tidy and well behaved simply won't say a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In order' seems to mean neat or correct; here it means a member of a monastic order, and the Cistercian monks of La Trappe are known for their vow of silence.
explanation.definitionFit: A monk of the Cistercian reform from La Trappe, an order famous for keeping silence.

clue.text: Dutchman who belonged to the Territorial Army ?

definitions.text: Dutchman who belonged to the Territorial Army ?

parts.words: Dutchman who belonged to the Territorial Army
parts.note: the seventeenth-century Dutch navigator, read as the man of the TA, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: A Dutch volunteer once served in the British reserve forces.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army (TA) is Britain's volunteer reserve; 'TA's man' spells the name of Abel Tasman, the Dutch explorer.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel Tasman, the Dutch explorer who reached Tasmania and New Zealand.

clue.text: The short and simple of the poor " (Gray)

definitions.text: The short and simple of the poor

parts.words: The short and simple of the poor
parts.note: a quotation with a gap, from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

explanation.surface: A line from Gray's Elegy on the humble lives of the poor.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line of Gray's Elegy reads 'The short and simple annals of the poor'; the clue is a fill-in-the-blank.
explanation.definitionFit: Annals are yearly records or histories, here the plain chronicles of humble lives.

clue.text: The old hypocrite, to kiss perfunctorily and disapprove

parts.note: a peck is a quick, casual kiss
to sniff is to show disdain or disapproval

explanation.surface: An elderly hypocrite gives a quick kiss then turns up his nose.
explanation.walkthrough: Seth Pecksniff in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit is the classic sanctimonious hypocrite.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Mr Pecksniff, whose name became a byword for unctuous hypocrisy.

clue.text: Crazy handlers got about fifty in a deadly grip

indicators.note: about means the scrambled letters go around the other piece
crazy says the letters of handlers and got are thrown into disorder

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Mad baggage handlers seized about fifty people in a lethal grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' rearranges HANDLERS GOT, and 'about' puts L (fifty) inside the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrestling hold round the throat, and figuratively any grip that chokes.

clue.text: A tool for fitters on piecework ?

definitions.text: A tool for fitters on piecework ?

parts.words: A tool for fitters on piecework
parts.note: fitters on piecework sounds like paid factory workers, but here it is people fitting pieces of a puzzle together; also the saw used to cut those pieces

explanation.surface: A workshop tool supplied to fitters who are paid by the piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piecework' suggests pay by output; the 'fitters' are puzzlers fitting cut pieces, and a fine saw of the same name cuts the curved shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle of interlocking cut pieces, and the fine fretsaw used to cut them, share this name.

clue.text: Lines hoisted in diametrically different ways

indicators.note: in a down clue hoisted means the letters are read upwards
in shows the letters sit inside the words diametrically different

explanation.surface: Lines hung up in completely opposite ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' finds LLYDI across 'diametricaLLY DIfferent', and 'hoisted' reads it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is a short pastoral poem, so a set of verses.

clue.text: This picture's stolen ?

parts.note: stolen sounds like an art theft but means taken quickly, a photograph snatched in an instant

explanation.surface: A gallery reports that a painting has been stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stolen' suggests theft; the picture is quickly taken, and 'snap' means grab as well as photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal photograph taken quickly with a hand camera.

clue.text: Something nasty in there at Cold Comfort Farm

definitions.text: Something nasty in there at Cold Comfort Farm

parts.words: Something nasty in there at Cold Comfort Farm
parts.note: Aunt Ada Doom in Stella Gibbons's novel once saw something nasty in a farm outbuilding

explanation.surface: Something unpleasant lurks at a bleak farm.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stella Gibbons's comic novel Cold Comfort Farm, Aunt Ada Doom's refrain is that she 'saw something nasty' in this outbuilding.
explanation.definitionFit: A shed for storing firewood, the place of Aunt Ada's famous fright.

clue.text: That's the position, no work without legal remedy

parts.note: sine is the Latin for without, familiar from legal phrases such as sine die
a cure is a remedy

explanation.surface: A lawyer describes a situation with no work done and no remedy available in law.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase 'sine cura', without care, gave the word for a paid post with no duties.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinecure is a paid office demanding little or no work.

clue.text: Many return in the same machine

indicators.note: in puts the reversed word inside the other piece

parts.note: DO, short for ditto, means the same again

indicators.note: return tells us the word Many is to be read backwards

explanation.surface: Many people come back inside the same machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns MANY into YNAM, and 'in' places it inside DO (ditto, 'the same').
explanation.definitionFit: A dynamo is a machine that generates electric current.

clue.text: What the President has is superior to housemaid's knee

definitions.text: What the President has is superior to housemaid's knee

parts.words: What the President has is superior to housemaid's knee
parts.note: a presiding officer's office, read as the presiding man's hip, a joint above a knee, as a master is above a maid

explanation.surface: A medical comparison of a President's ailment with a servant's.
explanation.walkthrough: Housemaid's knee is an inflamed kneecap from scrubbing floors; split the answer as 'chairman's hip': a hip is above a knee, and a chairman ranks above a housemaid.
explanation.definitionFit: The office held by whoever presides over a meeting or board.

clue.text: Heaven-propping mountains

definitions.meaning: in Greek myth the Titan who holds up the sky on his shoulders
the range of North Africa bearing the Titan's name

explanation.surface: Mountains so tall they seem to hold up the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titan condemned to support the heavens, and the North African mountain range named after him.

clue.text: They make nothing of other philosophies

definitions.text: They make nothing of other philosophies

parts.words: They make nothing of other philosophies
parts.note: people who dismiss rival views, and also believers in nothing, from Latin nihil

explanation.surface: Some thinkers are dismissive of every philosophy but their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make nothing of' means dismiss; it also points to Latin nihil, nothing, the root of the word for those who reject all values.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of a creed that denies all moral and religious values, believing in nothing.

clue.text: Sound cue for giving a ring

definitions.text: Sound cue for giving a ring

parts.words: Sound cue for giving a ring
parts.note: giving a ring sounds like proposing marriage, but means making a telephone call, which waits on a signal heard in the receiver

explanation.surface: A cue to a suitor to produce an engagement ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giving a ring' is British for making a phone call; the hum on lifting the receiver tells you to begin.
explanation.definitionFit: The continuous tone heard in a telephone receiver, telling the caller the line is ready.

clue.text: The silly goose was he who killed its producer

definitions.text: The silly goose was he who killed its producer

parts.words: The silly goose was he who killed its producer
parts.note: the fable of the man who killed the goose that laid treasure, hoping to get it all at once

explanation.surface: Only a fool would kill the goose that keeps laying.
explanation.walkthrough: In Aesop's fable the farmer kills his goose to get all its treasure at once and gets none; 'silly goose' is the man, and the goose is the producer.
explanation.definitionFit: The precious egg laid daily by the fabled goose, a source of steady wealth.

clue.text: How tears ran, when swindled out of a pound

indicators.note: swindled out of reads as the pound being held within the swindling

parts.note: tricked means swindled
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: Someone wept after being cheated of a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swindled out of a pound' puts L (a pound) inside TRICKED.
explanation.definitionFit: Tears trickle when they flow slowly in drops.

clue.text: Maybe hanging's wrong, despite this show of anger

indicators.note: wrong says the letters are put into the wrong order

explanation.surface: Perhaps hanging is wrong, yet someone shows fury over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges HANGINGS, the 's' of 'hanging's' counted as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Grinding the teeth is a sign of rage.

clue.text: Like the average sample the young Tullivers had at home

definitions.text: the young Tullivers had at home
definitions.meaning: Tom and Maggie Tulliver of George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss grew up at Dorlcote Mill, free to roam it

explanation.surface: A survey contrasts an average sample with the household of the Tulliver children.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tullivers are the family of George Eliot's novel The Mill on the Floss; their children had free run of their father's mill.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary or mediocre, and also the freedom of the family mill that Tom and Maggie enjoyed.

clue.text: Lift to ventilate cask and find fur

indicators.note: in a down clue lift means the whole phrase is read upwards

parts.note: to air is to ventilate
a tun is a large cask

explanation.surface: An instruction to raise a barrel to let air in and find fur inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' reads AIR TUN upwards as NUTRIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutria is the pelt of the coypu, a South American rodent.

clue.text: Backings with the bookmakers

parts.note: backings sounds like bets placed with bookies, but means the backs that book makers bind

explanation.surface: Bets placed with the bookmakers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backings' and 'bookmakers' suggest betting; it is bookbinders who make the backs of books.
explanation.definitionFit: The bound back edges of books, which carry the title.

clue.text: An Englishman's home ruler ?

parts.note: the proverb says an Englishman's home is his castle, so its ruler is a castle governor

explanation.surface: Who is master in an Englishman's house?
explanation.walkthrough: The British proverb 'an Englishman's home is his castle' turns the home into a castle, whose keeper has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A castellan is the governor or keeper of a castle.

clue.text: Dodge the end of the Bach piece

indicators.note: the end of means only the tail of the word is kept, losing its start

parts.note: a prelude is a piece by Bach, as in his preludes and fugues

explanation.surface: Avoid the end of the Bach composition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the end of' keeps the tail of PRELUDE, dropping PR.
explanation.definitionFit: To elude is to evade or escape skilfully.

clue.text: Fit of pique perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of pique may be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A sudden fit of resentment, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit of pique' is a phrase, but 'Fit' is the definition and 'perhaps' shuffles PIQUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To equip is to fit out or furnish with what is needed.

clue.text: Indisposed to describe eagles' eggs?

definitions.meaning: eggs that eagles have produced and stored high in their eyrie

explanation.surface: Feeling unwell and asked to describe the eggs of eagles.
explanation.definitionFit: Confined by illness, and also deposited and kept, as eggs high in a nest.

clue.text: Where some play follow my leader at the double?

definitions.text: Where some play follow my leader at the double

parts.words: Where some play follow my leader at the double
parts.note: the children's game of following a leader suits flocks, which trot one after another across pasture

explanation.surface: A playground where children run the game of follow-my-leader.
explanation.walkthrough: Follow-my-leader is a children's game; sheep notoriously follow the leader, and at the double means running.
explanation.definitionFit: A tract of grazing land where a flock is pastured.

clue.text: He'd have to put in some spade-work to get through to the English !

definitions.text: He'd have to put in some spade-work to get through to the English !

parts.words: He'd have to put in some spade-work to get through to the English
parts.note: an Australian, nicknamed after the gold-field miners, would have to dig through the earth to reach England on the far side

explanation.surface: An outsider must work hard to make the English understand him.
explanation.walkthrough: Australian soldiers were called by this nickname; England lies on the opposite side of the globe, so one would dig straight through to reach it.
explanation.definitionFit: An Australian, by the nickname from gold-field miners, and anyone who excavates with a spade.

clue.text: It's handy for sightseeing with intelligence ?

definitions.text: It's handy for sightseeing with intelligence ?

parts.words: It's handy for sightseeing with intelligence
parts.note: intelligence means espionage, so this is a hand-held lens for watching like a secret agent

explanation.surface: A guide that helps a clever tourist enjoy the sights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intelligence' looks like cleverness but means spying; the instrument is a small hand-held telescope.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hand-held telescope for viewing distant things.
